topic: Ignaz Semmelweis: the doctor who was mocked for saying 'wash your hands'
script:
In the 1840s, in one of the most advanced hospitals in the world, women would beg on their knees not to be taken to a certain ward.

Some of them were so afraid that they gave birth in the street, outside the hospital gates, rather than be admitted on the wrong day.

They knew something the doctors didn't want to believe. In that ward, mothers were dying at a terrifying rate. And the cause was something so simple, so ordinary, that when one young doctor finally figured it out, his colleagues laughed at him, pushed him out, and he ended his life locked away.

His discovery was this: doctors should wash their hands.

This is the story of Ignaz Semmelweis.

The year is 1846. Vienna. The Vienna General Hospital is enormous and famous, a place where doctors from all over Europe come to train. It has a maternity department split into two clinics. Women are admitted to one or the other on alternating days.

On paper, the two clinics are the same. Same building. Same kind of patients. But they are run differently. The First Clinic is where doctors and medical students deliver babies. The Second Clinic is run by midwives.

And in the First Clinic, a disease called childbed fever is killing mothers. In some years, around one in ten women who gave birth there died. In some terrible months, it was far worse. In the Second Clinic, run by the midwives, the death rate was a fraction of that.

Everyone in Vienna knew it. The women knew it. That's why they begged. That's why some of them preferred to give birth in the street. And here's a detail that should have been a giant clue: the women who gave birth in the street, on the way to the hospital, were much less likely to catch the fever than the women delivered by the doctors inside.

A twenty-eight-year-old Hungarian doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis became obsessed with this question. Why? Why was the doctors' clinic so much deadlier than the midwives' clinic?

At the time, most doctors believed diseases were caused by bad air, or by something mysterious in the atmosphere, or by the patient's own body. Semmelweis did something unusual for his time. He collected data, and he tested ideas one at a time.

Was it overcrowding? No, the Second Clinic was actually more crowded.

Was it the weather? No, both clinics had the same weather.

Was it the position women gave birth in? He changed it. Nothing happened.

There was even a theory that the women were frightened to death by a priest who walked through the First Clinic ringing a bell when he came to give last rites. So Semmelweis asked the priest to take a different route, quietly, with no bell. The deaths continued.

Nothing worked. And then, in 1847, tragedy gave him the answer.

Semmelweis had a close friend and colleague named Jakob Kolletschka, a professor who performed autopsies. During one examination, a student accidentally cut Kolletschka's finger with a scalpel. Within days, Kolletschka became very ill, and then he died.

When Semmelweis read the report on his friend's death, he noticed something chilling. The findings looked almost exactly like those of the mothers dying of childbed fever.

And suddenly, everything clicked.

In the First Clinic, doctors and students often began their day in the autopsy room, studying the bodies of patients who had died. Then they walked straight to the maternity ward to examine women in labor. They didn't wash their hands properly in between. Why would they? Nobody knew about germs yet.

The midwives in the Second Clinic never did autopsies.

Semmelweis concluded that the doctors were carrying something from the autopsy room on their hands, he called it cadaverous particles, and passing it to the mothers. The doctors themselves were spreading the disease.

In May 1847, he introduced a new rule. Before examining patients, every doctor and student had to wash their hands in a solution of chlorinated lime, a kind of chlorine disinfectant. He chose chlorine because it removed the smell of the autopsy room, and he reasoned that if the smell was gone, whatever caused the disease might be gone too.

The results were astonishing. In the months before the rule, the death rate in the First Clinic had been as high as about eighteen percent. Within a short time, it dropped to around two percent, and at times even lower. Mothers stopped dying. Just like that.

This should have been the happy ending. A young doctor had found a simple, almost free way to save thousands of lives. All anyone had to do was wash their hands.

Instead, it was the beginning of his downfall.

Many senior doctors were offended. Semmelweis was essentially telling them that they, the respected physicians, had been responsible for the deaths of their own patients. Some reportedly argued that a gentleman's hands were clean. Others simply didn't believe it, because his explanation didn't fit the medical theories of the time. He couldn't show them the cause, because nobody could yet see germs.

It didn't help that Semmelweis was slow to publish his findings, and that when he did argue for them, he could be blunt, angry, and impatient. He made powerful enemies.

In 1849, his position at the hospital was not renewed. He eventually left Vienna and returned to Hungary, to the city of Pest, now part of Budapest. There, at a small hospital, he introduced handwashing again, and again the death rate of mothers fell dramatically.

In 1861, he finally published a full book on his discovery. Many reviews were harsh. Leading doctors across Europe dismissed it. Frustrated and furious, Semmelweis wrote open letters to his critics, accusing them of letting women die.

Over the next few years, his behavior became more and more erratic. Historians still debate exactly what was wrong. It may have been an illness affecting his brain, or the toll of years of rejection.

In 1865, his colleagues had him committed to an asylum near Vienna. He was tricked into going, told he was visiting a new institute. When he realized where he was and tried to leave, he was beaten by the guards.

Two weeks later, Ignaz Semmelweis was dead. He was forty-seven years old. The cause was an infected wound on his hand, most likely from that beating. The man who had fought to stop deadly infections died from one.

And here's the cruelest part. Just a few years later, the world caught up.

In the 1860s, the French scientist Louis Pasteur was showing that microscopic germs cause disease. In 1867, the British surgeon Joseph Lister began using antiseptics in surgery, and infections plummeted. Germ theory explained exactly what Semmelweis had seen. He had been right all along. He just didn't live to see anyone admit it.

Today, Semmelweis is remembered as a pioneer of hand hygiene and infection control. A university in Budapest carries his name. And there's even a term in psychology called the Semmelweis reflex. It describes our tendency to reject new evidence, simply because it contradicts what we already believe.

So the next time you wash your hands, take a second to think about Ignaz Semmelweis. Something that takes twenty seconds, something we teach to small children, was once an idea so controversial that it destroyed the man who discovered it.

youtube.title: The Doctor They Locked Away for Saying 'Wash Your Hands'
youtube.description:
In 1840s Vienna, women begged not to be taken to one maternity ward - because there, mothers were dying of childbed fever at a terrifying rate.

A young doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis figured out why: doctors were going straight from autopsies to deliveries without washing their hands. When he made them wash in chlorinated lime, deaths dropped from around 18% to about 2%.

His reward? Mockery, the end of his career, and a tragic death in an asylum - just years before germ theory proved him right.
